sections.heading: How does chronic kidney disease feel and progress?
sections.body:
Early chronic kidney disease usually causes no symptoms, and it is often found by chance when a blood or urine test is done for another reason. Symptoms can appear at a more advanced stage, including tiredness, swollen ankles, feet or hands, shortness of breath, feeling sick and blood in the urine. Later kidney failure can also bring itching, muscle cramps and changes in how often a person passes urine.

Doctors describe the condition in stages, and a higher stage means more severe disease. In stage 1 the filtering is normal but there is other evidence of kidney damage, and stage 2 is a slight decrease in function. Stage 3 is split into 3a and 3b, stage 4 is a further fall, and stage 5 is known as established kidney failure. Only a small proportion of people with the condition go on to kidney failure, which the NHS puts at around 2 in 100 people. When the kidneys do stop working, this usually happens gradually, so there is time to plan the next stage of treatment.

sections.heading: How is it checked and followed up?
sections.body:
Chronic kidney disease can be diagnosed with blood and urine tests. The blood test is used to estimate how well the kidneys are filtering, and the urine test looks for protein and blood. Once the condition is diagnosed, kidney function is followed with regular blood and urine tests.

Some people are tested more often, including those taking long-term medicines that can affect the kidneys, such as lithium, omeprazole or anti-inflammatory painkillers called NSAIDs. The condition commonly affects blood pressure, red blood cell counts and bone health, so these may be checked as well. A referral to a dietitian is common, so that diet advice can fit the person. The NHS says most people with the condition can control it with medicine and regular check-ups.

sections.heading: What treatments are used?
sections.body:
There is no cure for chronic kidney disease, but treatment can help relieve the symptoms and stop it getting worse. The NHS describes lifestyle changes to stay as healthy as possible, together with medicines to manage problems such as high blood pressure and high cholesterol. ACE inhibitors are commonly used for blood pressure in this condition, and statins may be prescribed to lower the risk of heart and blood vessel problems.

Anaemia, a shortage of red blood cells, is common, and most people with kidney disease are given iron because it is needed to make red blood cells. Further anaemia treatment may involve a medicine called erythropoietin. Medicines can also be used for other symptoms of kidney failure, such as breathlessness, loss of appetite and itchy skin.

sections.heading: What are dialysis and a kidney transplant?
sections.body:
For a small number of people the kidneys eventually stop working, and dialysis or a transplant is then considered. Dialysis is a way of removing waste products and extra fluid from the blood. NIDDK describes haemodialysis as running the blood through an external filter by machine, while peritoneal dialysis uses the lining of the abdomen as the filter inside the body.

A kidney transplant is the other main option, and the kidney can come from a living or a deceased donor. NHS Blood and Transplant says living donors account for roughly 30 in 100 kidney transplants, with a much shorter wait than for a kidney from a deceased donor. People with a transplant take anti-rejection medicines for as long as the new kidney works, and NIDDK notes these can cause other health problems. Some people choose not to have dialysis or a transplant, or these may not suit them, and supportive care then aims to control symptoms with medical, psychological and practical support.

sections.heading: Living with chronic kidney disease
sections.body:
The NHS says many people with the condition live long lives without being unduly affected by it. Looking after general health still matters, particularly to reduce the risk of heart disease and stroke. Lifestyle advice includes stopping smoking for those who smoke and keeping physically active. Guidance favours plenty of fruit, vegetables and pulses, with smaller amounts of animal protein such as meat, fish and eggs.

It also advises limiting salt, and diet advice from a dietitian is individual and changes as the disease progresses. Regular ibuprofen-type painkillers are best avoided because they can affect kidney function. People are advised to check with their care team before starting a new exercise programme.

sections.heading: Complications and outlook
sections.body:
Heart and blood vessel disease is a major concern in chronic kidney disease. Research summaries note that people with the condition are more likely to die of heart and blood vessel complications than to reach kidney failure. Anaemia is widespread, and it becomes more common as kidney disease advances.

Bone problems can also develop, because the balance of calcium, phosphate and vitamin D in the body is disturbed. Because of these links, treatment looks at the heart, the blood and the bones as well as the kidneys. NHS 111 Wales gives the proportion who reach kidney failure as around 1 in 50 people. For most people the outlook depends on controlling the condition with medicine and regular check-ups.

faqs.q: Can chronic kidney disease be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure for chronic kidney disease, but treatment can help relieve symptoms and stop it getting worse. The NHS says most people can control the condition with medicine and regular check-ups. Looking after general health, especially to lower the risk of heart disease and stroke, still matters. Many people live long lives without being unduly affected.

faqs.q: Does it always lead to kidney failure?
faqs.a: No, only a small proportion of people do. The NHS says around 2 in 100 people with the condition reach kidney failure. When it does happen it is usually gradual, so there is time to plan the next stage of treatment, such as dialysis or a transplant.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the two kinds of dialysis?
faqs.a: Dialysis removes waste products and extra fluid from the blood. In haemodialysis, a machine runs the blood through an external filter. In peritoneal dialysis, the lining of the abdomen acts as the filter inside the body. A kidney team discusses the options before they are needed.

faqs.q: Does everyone with kidney failure have dialysis or a transplant?
faqs.a: No, some people choose not to, and these treatments may not suit everyone. In that case the aim of supportive care is to treat and control the symptoms of kidney failure. This still includes medical, psychological and practical support. Both dialysis and a transplant are discussed with the person before they are needed.

faqs.q: Which painkillers can affect the kidneys?
faqs.a: Regular ibuprofen-type painkillers can affect kidney function, so avoiding them is advised. People on long-term medicines that can affect the kidneys, such as lithium, omeprazole or anti-inflammatory painkillers called NSAIDs, are tested more often. This testing is done with blood and urine tests.

faqs.q: Does diet matter in chronic kidney disease?
faqs.a: Guidance favours plenty of fruit, vegetables and pulses, with smaller amounts of animal protein such as meat, fish and eggs. Limiting salt is also advised. Diet advice is individual and changes as the condition progresses, so a dietitian referral is common.
